repos.title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary:
D3D is a standalone diffusion drafter for speculative decoding that does not need updated target-model hidden states, so the next draft block can be computed during target verification. It is initialized from a pretrained autoregressive model and trained on target-generated responses with blockwise denoising (block size 16) plus an auxiliary autoregressive loss. Layers are then pruned one at a time using validation acceptance length, with distillation-based recovery training. At inference, one packed drafter pass prepares continuations for possible rejection outcomes and full acceptance. A cache hit reuses a prepared branch; a miss triggers synchronous drafting.

On seven benchmarks with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, D3D averages 5.00× and 5.71× decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding. DFlash averages 4.03× and 3.67×, and DSpark averages 4.44× and 3.92×. The peak is 7.48× on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B. Average acceptance length at block size 16 is 7.88 (Qwen3-8B) and 7.73 (Qwen3-32B). Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks.

Limitations: the main comparison uses two GPUs (one for the target, one for the drafter), and per-GPU throughput is not compared. The drafter adds memory, cache misses stall verification, and experiments use the Transformers backend rather than SGLang or vLLM.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Target-conditioned drafters must wait for fresh target states, so drafting and verification run sequentially.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior drafters mostly condition on target features, whereas D3D trains without them and prunes layers.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: D3D trains a standalone drafter, prunes layers by acceptance loss, and prepares successor blocks during verification.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: D3D averages 5.00× and 5.71× decoding speedup, above DFlash's 4.03× and 3.67×, on seven benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors claim the first empirical demonstration of asynchronous lossless speculative decoding with a standalone diffusion drafter.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations are the extra drafter memory, synchronous drafting on cache misses, and no test in production serving frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the teacher-adjustment formula, extra ablations on training weight, block size and anchors, and selective prefilling on LongBench.

repos.title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
repos.paper_summary: LExMem is a graph-guided benchmark for long-term memory in exploration tasks, where a model must track trial-and-error progress toward a goal, including revisions and revived attempts. The benchmark models exploration as directed graphs, evolves them with mutation rules, and instantiates them as 224 multi-turn dialogues (research and software design domains) with 2,018 QA instances in three types: dense subgraphs, sparse subgraphs, and same-type sets. The paper also proposes LExGraph, which segments dialogue into memory nodes with summary-and-fact keys, links them by hierarchical and cross-branch edges, and retrieves nodes by fusing embedding and BM25 rankings, then expanding to neighbors. On LExMem, LExGraph reaches 0.667 F1 and 63.92 ACC on Same-Type questions with Qwen-3.8 27B, versus 0.624 F1 and 61.67 overall ACC for the strongest baseline, LightRAG; the paper reports p<0.05 with paired bootstrap. Limitations: the dialogues are synthetic, and the benchmark tests memory via QA rather than whether recalled memory improves downstream exploration decisions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing memory benchmarks test recall of facts, so the paper builds LExMem for iterative exploration and LExGraph for memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Curation
digest_headlines.headline: Graph-guided synthesis turns evolved graphs into 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances across three question types.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph links dialogue segments into memory nodes with hierarchical and cross-branch edges, then retrieves by hybrid scoring.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setting
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph is compared with five retrieval-based and three memory-based baselines using token overlap and a judge-scored accuracy metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph achieves the highest overall LExMem performance across backbones and keeps an advantage on all question subsets.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior memory benchmarks and frameworks target fact recall or semantic and entity links, not the progression of exploration.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Existing frameworks struggle on LExMem, while LExGraph improves on strong baselines and transfers to an external long-term memory benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits are synthetic dialogues and question answering that does not test whether memory improves downstream exploration decisions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists mutation rules, seed task details, evidence annotation, human evaluation, baseline settings, evidence retrieval results and capability definitions.

repos.title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces CaRT+, a daily lumped catchment model with 14 states and 35 parameters per catchment. It is built under three hydrological laws (conservation, dissipation, aggregation) and refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. The model contains no neural network. Each refinement targets a deficit diagnosed from observations and is kept only if paired comparisons on a development split improve. Evaluation covers 602 gauged British and 593 gauged US catchments, with training in 1989–2008 and testing in 2011–2019. Median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency for single models is 0.863 (GB) and 0.765 (US) for CaRT+, against 0.869 and 0.751 for a stateful LSTM and 0.862 and 0.754 for an entity-aware LSTM. On 505 gauged Australian catchments not used in development, CaRT+ reaches 0.778, against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. Limitations: three-seed LSTM ensembles stay ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003–0.012 median NSE; the paper reports gaps in low flows and in arid held-out catchments; internal states are not checked against soil moisture or groundwater; and the learned closure depends on the training climate.

digest_headlines.heading: Plain Language Summary
digest_headlines.headline: Three physical laws constrain catchment models, and a simple model without a neural network matches deep learning on about 1900 catchments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Deep-learning models outperform process-based models on streamflow, so the question is whether a low-dimensional structure built under physical laws can match them.

digest_headlines.heading: Hydrological laws
digest_headlines.headline: Three laws, conservation, dissipation and aggregation, fix the form of a lumped model and admit four kinds of refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: A base model
digest_headlines.headline: CaRT, a base model with one store per process class, uses 11 parameters per catchment and is regionalised by a static network.

digest_headlines.heading: Refining the base model
digest_headlines.headline: Refinements target observed deficits, such as quick-flow connectivity and frost, and each is kept if it improves development-split comparisons.

digest_headlines.heading: Results on CAMELS-GB, CAMELS-US and CAMELS-AUS
digest_headlines.headline: Single CaRT+ and stateful LSTM models reach 0.863 and 0.869 median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency in Britain, and 0.765 and 0.751 in the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Known processes assembled under the laws suffice for streamflow accuracy, but the internal states and fluxes still need independent observations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: One 35-parameter structure matches single LSTMs on 1342 catchments and transfers to 561 Australian ones, supporting laws of form.

digest_headlines.heading: Open Research
digest_headlines.headline: Data sources, an Australian dataset release and the code for CaRT and CaRT+ are listed with their repository and record identifiers.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix derives the memory that aggregation leaves, the conditions under which few states carry it, and the daily numerical schemes.

repos.title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation
repos.paper_summary: NanoKV is a frozen-backbone framework for high-ratio compression of the historical key-value (KV) cache in autoregressive video generation. It stores shared content in cluster centers and encodes joint head-channel residuals into INT4 coefficients. Keys and Values get different fitting objectives: Key decoders are trained with block-output alignment to preserve downstream block outputs, and Value codecs are trained through the quantization path to reconstruct residuals. The optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention. Evaluation covers HY-WorldPlay, Matrix-Game 3.5, and LingBot-World 2.0, using 400 videos per configuration from 100 VBench-I2V images with four camera actions each. On HY-WorldPlay at nominal 32× compression, NanoKV reaches 26.09× effective KV compression, versus 13.50× for KVTC, with PSNR 19.56 dB against 18.56 dB for KVTC. NanoKV-Fast reaches 20.53× with 19.04 dB PSNR and a 1.06× speedup over Original, versus 0.92× for KVTC. Fidelity is measured against matched uncompressed rollouts, not ground truth. The codecs are fitted per backbone, and NanoKV-Fast's low-dimensional approximation may accumulate errors over long horizons.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Growing KV history raises memory and attention costs, so NanoKV compresses historical KV while preserving downstream generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work selects history tokens, compresses features, or changes the model; NanoKV compresses retained features with a frozen backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Joint head–channel compression retains the most KV variance, and Key block-output alignment reduces mean output error by 15.3%.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: NanoKV stores shared centers and low-bit residual coefficients, fitting Key decoders by block-output alignment and Value codecs through quantization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV reaches 26.09× effective compression and 19.56 PSNR, against 13.50× and 18.56 for KVTC.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NanoKV improves the quality–storage trade-off across three backbones, but codec fitting and attention adaptation remain backbone-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers cache and baseline protocols, codec training and error diagnostics, memory and runtime accounting, and additional quality and example figures.

repos.title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
repos.paper_summary:
This paper re-evaluates Hawkes processes against neural temporal point processes (TPPs) under one protocol and releases TorchPP, an open-source PyTorch framework implementing both. Hawkes baselines get spline baselines, spline kernels, and an inhibitive variant. Neural models include THP, SAHP, NHP, IntensityFree, and NeuralSplineTPP, a Transformer with a spline intensity head. Evaluation uses autoregressive next-event prediction on five standard benchmarks, plus a 1,257-type UK Biobank disease-history task and a 117-type MIMIC-IV ICU task. Log-likelihood is split into a time term and a type-conditional term. Each model is run with five seeds, and mean and standard deviation are reported.

On the standard benchmarks, flexible Hawkes processes close most of the gap to neural TPPs. NeuralSplineTPP matches IntensityFree and outperforms the softplus-headed intensity models. Added intensity flexibility mainly improves the time term, not the type term. On MIMIC-IV, the flexible neural TPP keeps an advantage in both terms. On UK Biobank, flexible Hawkes processes nearly match the best neural TPP.

Limitations: only next-event prediction is assessed, conclusions rest on seven datasets, and the UK Biobank data and models are not released.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prior neural-versus-Hawkes comparisons used rigid Hawkes models and omitted medical data, so this paper re-evaluates them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Hawkes processes sum a baseline and pairwise kernels, while neural TPPs learn intensities from encoded event history.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Design
digest_headlines.headline: Hawkes models gain spline baselines and kernels, and neural models vary only the output head, all under one likelihood.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Flexible Hawkes models narrow most of the gap, and neural gains mainly appear in the time term rather than the type term.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Standard benchmarks look dominated by pairwise structure, so a flexible Hawkes process is a sensible practical starting point.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The reported gap was largely an artifact of under-specified models, and flexible intensities also limit neural TPPs.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from the European Research Council and Deutsche Krebshilfe, and both UK Biobank and MIMIC-IV access are acknowledged.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers implementation, EasyTPP comparison, Hawkes baseline reproduction, extra metrics, knot sweeps, and calibration.

repos.title: Online Adaptation to Latent Physical Properties for Learning from Demonstration
repos.paper_summary:
The paper proposes an imitation learning method for manipulating visually identical objects whose centers of mass (CoM) differ. A dynamics model and one learned scalar latent parameter per object type are trained jointly from demonstrations that include regrasping and contact-location changes. A Diffusion Policy is then conditioned on these parameters. During execution, the model and policy stay fixed, and only the latent estimate is updated by gradient descent on prediction error, starting from a plausible initial value.

Experiments use two real-robot tasks (Pouch Placement, Box Pushing) and one simulated task (Horizontal Lifting), each with three training seeds. The baseline is a Diffusion Policy trained on pooled demonstrations. Online adaptation improves task success rates, but in simulation, success on CoM locations absent from the demonstrations stays around 30%. Retraining the VAE and dynamics model on rollout data further improves success while the policy stays fixed.

Limitations: CoM varies in one dimension only, the latent is scalar, and estimates from brief interactions are not always reliable. For Box Pushing, the learned representations do not always yield the lowest prediction error for the matching object.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Adaptive manipulation needs information gathered through interaction, which this work pairs with learning from demonstration.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work estimates physical properties through exploration or observation history, while this method updates only a latent representation online.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: A dynamics model and a per-object latent parameter are learned from demonstrations, then only that parameter is updated during deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use two real-robot tasks and one simulation task, with objects whose centers of mass differ and held-out positions.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: Online adaptation raised pouch placement success from 40.7% to 66.7% and reached 32.5% on unseen lifting positions.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Estimates from brief interaction are sometimes unreliable, and success on unseen centers of mass stayed around 30%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Latent physical representations updated online can improve imitation, but adaptation to unseen configurations stayed limited.

repos.title: The Harness Is the Model: Agent Scaffolding Changes a Fixed LLM's Compliance with Banking Conduct Rules, Unevenly Across Models
repos.paper_summary:
This paper tests whether the agent harness around a fixed language model changes compliance with banking conduct rules. Four open-weight models each ran five harnesses (a fixed-workflow pipeline, a ReAct tool loop, a policy reachable only by search, a long benign customer memory, and a same-model reviewer) on 156 cases in a simulated retail bank with 11 rule families that paraphrase EU provisions. Violations and over-refusals were scored deterministically from executed tool calls, giving 3120 episodes. Pooled correct-case rates ranged from 87.3% to 92.1%. Within one model, the harness spread was 11.5 points (Cochran's Q=25.1, p<0.001), while another model showed no detectable effect. The model-by-harness interaction was not significant (p=0.07). The same-model reviewer cut violations from 9.6% to 6.4% without raising over-refusals. Date-arithmetic rules failed in every harness. In an exploratory analysis, 26% of violations came with a customer message denying the executed action.

Limitations: the bank and policy are synthetic, some rules are stricter than the law they paraphrase, only four moderate open-weight models without reasoning were tested, and the interaction test is underpowered.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Deployed banking assistants are a model inside a harness, and the study varies only the harness to test conduct compliance.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks hold the harness fixed or report small scaffold effects, leaving conduct rules under controlled harness variation untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Four open-weight models ran five harnesses on 156 cases in a simulated bank, scored deterministically from executed actions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Harness effects were significant for two models and absent for one, and the model-by-harness interaction was not significant at 5%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The model-harness pair is the unit to validate, and conduct testing should read the executed action log rather than the conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The synthetic bank, one policy, four moderate open-weight models and judge-based analysis limit how far results generalise.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: With the model fixed, the harness changed violation rates and rankings, and 26% of violations were invisible in conversations.

digest_headlines.heading: Declarations
digest_headlines.headline: The declarations cover funding, a competing interest, public code and traces, and how AI tools were used.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix A. Rule families and legal sources
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix A lists eleven rule families with the European provisions they paraphrase and notes where the manual is stricter.

repos.title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
repos.paper_summary: SysPilot is a cross-library autotuner built on Library Performance Contracts (LPCs), reusable per-library specifications written in the LPCL language. Each contract declares a library's components, the shared resources they use (such as CPU compute and GPU memory), assumptions, controls, and runtime signals. SysPilot composes an application's library contracts, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the workload to validate them, and generates candidate configurations only for validated hypotheses. An LLM pipeline drafts contracts from documentation and code, and the output is checked against the LPCL grammar. On LibContentionBench, nine cross-library contention benchmarks, SysPilot reaches an average normalized score of 0.960, versus 0.824 for SMAC3 and 0.729 for OpenTuner, and reaches a 0.8 score in 3× fewer trials. On a LibTorch partitioning example, it finds the best configuration in 7 trials, versus 26 for OpenTuner and 45 for SMAC3. Limitations: contract quality depends on documentation, composition is conservative and can yield false positives and negatives, and version and build differences are not handled.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Library composition causes cross-library resource contention, and SysPilot tunes it using reusable per-library performance contracts.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: A two-task LibTorch example shows generic autotuners need 26 and 45 trials, while library-level information finds the best configuration in 7.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: SysPilot complements existing resource-control mechanisms and differs from black-box autotuners by using a structured representation to narrow the search.

digest_headlines.heading: Design
digest_headlines.headline: Library Performance Contracts describe a library's resource use, controls, and signals, and SysPilot composes them into conflict hypotheses.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: A large language model pipeline generates LPCL contracts from documentation and code, and virtual probes keep contracts platform-independent.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Across nine benchmarks, contract-guided tuning reaches an average normalized score of 0.960 at 30 trials, above SMAC3 at 0.824 and OpenTuner at 0.729.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: SysPilot's results depend on contract quality, conservative composition may produce false positives or miss undocumented interference, and version sensitivity is not fully handled.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Proposed extensions include version-aware contracts and distributed workflow tuning, beyond the current single-node focus.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Library contracts with profiling validation find better configurations in fewer trials than generic autotuners.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the nine benchmarks' libraries, datasets, shared resources, configuration-space sizes, and best performance gains.

repos.title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
repos.paper_summary: ProcessPrefBench is a benchmark for testing whether an assistant can carry a user's process preference from one dialogue into a different task that does not restate it. The preferences come from three months of natural dialogues between two knowledge workers and an AI-discussion product, and the benchmark has 66 source–target cases. Each source is preselected, so the test measures application rather than retrieval. Three models (DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen-Max, GPT-4o) were run under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts, with two generations per case. Judging used a Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge scoring preference realization on a 0–2 rubric, plus a separate task gate. Imperative distilled-preference prompting raised preference scores over target-only prompting by 0.244 points (95% CI [0.177, 0.313]); full-history prompting gained 0.204. Distillation showed no reliable advantage over full history (difference +0.026, p=.451). Fabricated-evidence failures rose from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.4% under imperative prompting and 10.1% under full history. Limitations: two users, one product, and a human audit of only 30 answers that does not validate the fabrication contrast.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Users reveal process preferences in dialogue, and ProcessPrefBench tests whether an assistant applies one learned in an earlier dialogue to a new task.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks test either memory of dialogue or stated preferences, not whether a preference induced from dialogue transfers to a new task.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Each case pairs a source dialogue supporting a reusable standard with a same-user target that does not restate it.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Three models are tested under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts, with 1980 answers generated in total.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompts raise preference scores over target-only prompting, but imperative prompting also raises fabricated-evidence failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Relevant history improves preference realization, but preserving the right standard and avoiding imported content remain separate requirements.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark rests on two users and 66 cases, and the judge audit is diagnostic, so effects hold under the benchmark judge.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics and Privacy
digest_headlines.headline: Natural interaction traces are not released until participant consent, privacy, provenance, and redistribution rights are reviewed.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and Code Availability
digest_headlines.headline: A public repository holds the benchmark definition, protocols, and schema now, while prompts, code, and case data await review.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the scoring protocol, judge calibration, sensitivity analyses, two end-to-end case audits, and fabricated-evidence examples.

repos.title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
repos.paper_summary: Confucius4-R2T2 is a streaming speech recognition model built by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on about 1,500 hours of proprietary Chinese and English audio, with the pre-trained audio encoder and projector frozen. It is trained with Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) labels, a new target defined so that the emitted text never changes once output. The authors prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Training adds a Wait token where the model should defer, with teacher-generated LSP labels from 80 ms audio prefixes and noise, reverberation, and language-tag augmentation. The paper reports that streaming accuracy approaches the base model's full-context quality, with low emission lag and gains on languages not used in post-training. The stated limitations are that deployment performance and broader generalization remain open, and that the LSP label is conservative, so it biases the model toward later emission.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Revisions to emitted tokens waste downstream work, so the paper treats output stability as a hard requirement alongside accuracy and latency.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work measures revisions, applies commit rules at inference, or trains on stable targets, while inference rules leave agreement unlearned.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Streaming a full-context model is hard because timestamp targets force guesses and newly added audio can disturb earlier tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: Freezing the encoder, the method trains the decoder to emit a Wait token whenever the received audio does not determine the next token.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Data Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B has the highest normalized streamability, 0.493, among the models evaluated on 1,860 Buckeye utterances.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Two stages, supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement learning, train only the language decoder while the encoder and projector stay frozen.

digest_headlines.heading: Streaming Inference
digest_headlines.headline: Cache reuse, Wait-terminated decoding, bounded context and suffix verification reduce per-update cost without changing the trained model.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluations
digest_headlines.headline: R2T2 with U=1 has a total macro error of 5.76, below all three proprietary systems evaluated, and about 0.6 percentage points above full-context decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Adapting a full-context model gives stable streaming recognition with transfer beyond training languages, while deployment performance remains open for further evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix defines three hindsight prefix criteria, proves their containment and coincidence relations, and treats the longest stable prefix as a learning target.
